title: Leadership Looks Like This
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that leadership is a key difference between high- and low-performing schools and organizations, drawing on Jim Collins's finding that great institutions have certain kinds of leaders. He is careful to say leadership alone does not make a school great but enables and protects the curriculum, instruction, and teacher-leader systems that do. He then describes two paired traits, humility practiced as a discipline and boldness in staying focused on the mission, and ties them to Collins's Level 5 leadership as humble-boldness. The humble leader decentralizes herself in the story while relentlessly re-centering the organization on what matters most through repeated communication, such as weekly leader newsletters. It is a short, character-based portrait of leadership rather than a technique list.
points: Leadership is a dependable differentiator between strong and weak schools, even though it works by protecting the other things that make a school great.
Humility is a trainable discipline of reminding oneself that the leader is not the protagonist of the organization's story.
Boldness means fiercely and repeatedly re-centering on the mission, and guarding against confusion and priority creep.
The pairing matters: the target is humble-boldness, not either trait alone.
quotes: That statement sounds silly to the sophisticated reader. Isn’t it more complicated than that? Don’t systems-level differences in schools come from socioeconomics, or teacher preparation patterns, or labor structures? Jim Collins had similar skepticism of the role of leadership in “great” institutions, but when he examined the data, he couldn’t escape it: great organizations are great in part because they have certain kinds of leaders.

I call it a discipline on purpose: humility is more like a muscle that can be strengthened than it is a feature that is fixed. It comes from the lifting of the weight of that constant inward messaging where we repeat, “It is not about me. I am not the protagonist of the story of my students or of my school.

I now believe that humble leaders give us better, saner schools, better, saner families, and better, saner countries. We’ve all seen this play out. Egocentric leaders waste time, energy, and resources — their own and ours.

Critically, the deeply humble leader is not passive or weak. Even as she practices the habit of decentralizing her role in the story, she also fiercely re-centers herself, hour by hour, day by day, on the critical mission on which her organization is built.
Confusion, obfuscation, and priority creep are her sworn enemies. Her abiding purpose is to see the advancement of the long-term flourishing of human beings.
